nodes.name: Read the same cache two ways
nodes.summary: A new query changes the mixture of values, even when the cache stays fixed. In a two-position toy row, changing the query from 1 to 0 changes the attention output from 8 to 6.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Read the same cache two ways

A new query changes the mixture of values, even when the cache stays fixed. In a two-position toy row, changing the query from 1 to 0 changes the attention output from 8 to 6.

The scaled score is q·kᵢ/√d. Softmax turns these scores into weights that sum to one. Attention returns the sum of each weight times its value.

Take d = 1, keys 0 and ln(3), and values 2 and 10. For q = 1, exponentiating the scores gives 1 and 3. The weights are ¼ and ¾, and the weighted sum is ¼ × 2 + ¾ × 10 = 8. For q = 0, each exponent is 1 and the answer is (2 + 10)/2 = 6. A real decoder includes the current position among those it can attend to.

This is how different queries read the [[causal-cache]]. It also explains how [[shared-heads]] can share stored values while producing different answers. [Transformer, §3.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

nodes.name: What can the next token reuse?
nodes.summary: A causal decoder saves a key and a value for each past position at each attention layer. Appending a token cannot change what an earlier position could see, so its old projections remain valid.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# What can the next token reuse?

A causal decoder saves a key and a value for each past position at each attention layer. Appending a token cannot change what an earlier position could see, so its old projections remain valid.

Suppose the prompt says “The spare key is in the blue drawer. Open the …”. Prefill processes the prompt and stores its projections. During decode the new position computes its own query, key, and value. It appends its key and value and uses its query to score the eligible keys. The key determines how relevant a position is to this query. The value supplies what it contributes. Each new query needs fresh scores.

Follow [[attention-row]] to see the same cache return two different answers, then [[dense-budget]] to count what gets stored. [Transformer attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

nodes.name: Compress older positions
nodes.summary: DeepSeek‑V4‑Flash combines a detailed recent window with compressed global history. Forming summaries reduces the inventory of stored entries. Sparse selection reduces how many entries a query reads.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Compress older positions

DeepSeek‑V4‑Flash combines a detailed recent window with compressed global history. Forming summaries reduces the inventory of stored entries. Sparse selection reduces how many entries a query reads.

Compressed Sparse Attention (CSA) produces finer summaries and selects relevant ones for each query. Heavily Compressed Attention (HCA) uses coarser summaries and can read all of them. A model can therefore store many entries yet consult only a few on a particular step. Grouping positions also changes the detail represented by each entry.

V4.1‑Flash adds sharing across layers through [[shared-layers]]. Check the distinction between stored and selected entries in [[transfer-check]]. [DeepSeek‑V4‑Flash model card](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Flash)

nodes.name: Count a dense KV cache
nodes.summary: One token in the example MHA model adds 512 KiB. At 4,096 tokens the cache holds 2 GiB for one sequence. A dense decoding step still reads keys and values from the history.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Count a dense KV cache

One token in the example MHA model adds 512 KiB. At 4,096 tokens the cache holds 2 GiB for one sequence. A dense decoding step still reads keys and values from the history.

Multiply batch × tokens × layers × KV heads × head dimension × 2 arrays × bytes per number. Here one token costs 1 × 32 layers × 32 heads × 128 numbers × 2 arrays × 2 bytes = 524,288 bytes. At 8,192 tokens the total reaches 4 GiB. This counts the ideal KV tensors. Weights, temporary storage, and allocator overhead have separate budgets.

Try [[shared-heads]] to change just one factor. Use [[global-budget]] for an architecture with a different storage layout. [Fast Transformer Decoding](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150)

nodes.name: Price one compressed entry
nodes.summary: A V4.1‑Flash global entry has a 288-byte main vector and a 68-byte index key. Count the scale bytes as well as the packed four-bit values.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Price one compressed entry

A V4.1‑Flash global entry has a 288-byte main vector and a 68-byte index key. Count the scale bytes as well as the packed four-bit values.

For the 512-channel main vector, two four-bit values occupy one byte and each group of 16 channels shares one scale byte. The total is 512/2 + 512/16 = 288 bytes. For the 128-channel index key, groups of 32 share a scale byte, giving 128/2 + 128/32 = 68 bytes. The combined price is 356 bytes. The local sliding-window cache uses FP8.

Multiply this price by the global writer rate from [[shared-layers]] to get the [[global-budget]]. [DeepSeek‑V4.1‑Flash precision](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.19969v1) · [Reference implementation](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash/blob/main/inference/model.py)

nodes.name: Reconstruct 890 bytes per token
nodes.summary: DeepSeek reports 890 bytes of global KV per token for V4.1‑Flash. That is about one quarter of V4‑Flash’s corresponding global footprint at equal context length.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Reconstruct 890 bytes per token

DeepSeek reports 890 bytes of global KV per token for V4.1‑Flash. That is about one quarter of V4‑Flash’s corresponding global footprint at equal context length.

The two ingredients are [[entry-precision]] (288 + 68 = 356 bytes per global entry) and [[shared-layers]] (3 × ½ + 1 = 2.5 entries per token). Multiply them: 356 × 2.5 = 890 bytes per token. At exactly one million tokens this term is 890,000,000 bytes, or 890 decimal MB (about 849 MiB). The local window, weights, allocator overhead, and temporary activations consume additional memory. The reported one-eighth figure concerns persistent storage in a different comparison.

Return to [[dense-budget]] to compare what each formula counts before using the numbers. [Technical report](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.19969v1) · [Release announcement](https://api-docs.deepseek.com/news/news260910/)

nodes.name: Store a learned latent
nodes.summary: DeepSeek‑V2’s multi-head latent attention stores a compact learned vector per position plus a positional key. Head-specific projections can use that shared vector.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Store a learned latent

DeepSeek‑V2’s multi-head latent attention stores a compact learned vector per position plus a positional key. Head-specific projections can use that shared vector.

Let c = W↓h compress the token’s hidden state h. The content score qᵀ(W↑c) equals (W↑ᵀq)ᵀc. Moving the projection onto the query allows scoring directly against the stored latent. The positional key preserves rotary position information. This reduces how many numbers each position needs while retaining head-specific transformations.

Compare this representation with the explicit KV banks in [[shared-heads]]. Another dimension available for compression is the number of positions represented, explored in [[compressed-history]]. [DeepSeek‑V2, §2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2405.04434v5)

nodes.name: Share keys and values across heads
nodes.summary: Keep 32 query heads. With 8 KV heads, each group of four queries reads one KV bank. With one KV head, every query reads the same bank. Each query still computes its own attention weights.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Share keys and values across heads

Keep 32 query heads. With 8 KV heads, each group of four queries reads one KV bank. With one KV head, every query reads the same bank. Each query still computes its own attention weights.

In the [[dense-budget]] example, MHA (32 KV heads), GQA (8), and MQA (1) use 2 GiB, 512 MiB, and 64 MiB respectively at 4,096 tokens. At 8,192 tokens they use 4 GiB, 1 GiB, and 128 MiB. These are hypothetical architectures with equal layer count, head size, and precision. An existing MHA model would need training or adaptation to share heads this way.

Historically, MQA appeared in 2019 and GQA in 2023. A different way to share information across heads is [[latent-attention]]. [MQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02150) · [GQA paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.13245)

nodes.name: Let several layers read one global store
nodes.summary: In DeepSeek‑V4.1‑Flash, a Full layer writes global KV and selects positions. A Reindex layer reads shared KV and chooses new positions. A Reuse layer also reuses a preceding selection.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Let several layers read one global store

In DeepSeek‑V4.1‑Flash, a Full layer writes global KV and selects positions. A Reindex layer reads shared KV and chooses new positions. A Reuse layer also reuses a preceding selection.

Every layer computes its own attention query and retains its own 128-token local attention window. Of the global writers, three encoder layers each write one entry per pair of tokens; one decoder layer writes one entry per token. Averaged over a long sequence that is 3 × ½ + 1 = 2.5 entries per token across the network. A fractional average counts entries over many tokens.

Combine that rate with [[entry-precision]] to reconstruct the [[global-budget]]. Earlier [[compressed-history]] addresses how far back positions are represented. [CSA2 and model configuration, §§2.3 and 4.2.1](https://arxiv.org/html/2609.19969v1)

nodes.name: Predict what changes
nodes.summary: Start with 4,096 tokens and 8 KV heads in the toy model. Double the sequence length and halve the number of KV heads. Predict the memory cost before opening the linked explanation.

knowledgeMeta.content:
# Predict what changes

Start with 4,096 tokens and 8 KV heads in the toy model. Double the sequence length and halve the number of KV heads. Predict the memory cost before opening the linked explanation.

Check: in [[dense-budget]], the factors of 2 and ½ cancel. The result stays at 512 MiB. All 32 query heads still have a KV group to read. Now compare two designs that each read 512 global entries per query. If one stores a same-sized entry per token and the other stores one per four tokens, which cache grows faster?

Check: the first stores about four times as many entries over a long prefix. A read limit is insufficient to determine storage. Revisit [[compressed-history]] for the mechanism, then try explaining [[global-budget]] without looking up its two factors.

nodes.name: A fixed cache can give different answers
nodes.summary: The query determines the attention weights assigned to the stored values. Changing only the query can therefore change their weighted sum.

nodes.name: Dense KV storage grows linearly with context length
nodes.summary: For one sequence with 32 layers, 32 KV heads, head dimension 128 and two-byte elements, the key and value tensors require 524,288 bytes per token.

nodes.name: Query heads can share stored KV banks
nodes.summary: Reducing the KV-head count reduces stored keys and values while retaining a separate attention computation for each query head.

nodes.name: Heads can score a shared latent directly
nodes.summary: Moving the content-key projection onto the query preserves the dot product and allows heads to score a shared stored latent. A separate positional key preserves rotary position information.

nodes.name: Compression and selection change different counts
nodes.summary: Compressing positions changes how many global entries are stored. Selecting a subset changes how many entries a query reads.

nodes.name: Four global writers average 2.5 entries per token
nodes.summary: In V4.1‑Flash, three encoder layers each write one global entry per pair of tokens, and one decoder layer writes one per token. Their rates sum to 2.5 entries per token over a long sequence.

nodes.name: Packed values and scale bytes sum to 356 bytes
nodes.summary: In the V4.1‑Flash global cache, the 512-channel main vector uses 256 packed-value bytes and 32 scale bytes. The 128-channel index key uses 64 packed-value bytes and four scale bytes.

nodes.name: Global KV grows by 890 bytes per token

The article works through the equality between projecting the latent and applying the transposed projection to the query.
CSA selects among finer summaries, while HCA can read all of its coarser summaries.
The article counts writers across layers that share their global cache and retain separate 128-token local windows.
The article prices the main vector at 288 bytes and the index key at 68 bytes, then sums them.

DeepSeek‑V2 is the named model in the worked latent-projection example.
V4‑Flash combines compressed history with selective reads in CSA.
The stated writer schedule is attributed specifically to DeepSeek‑V4.1‑Flash.
The article links arXiv 1911.02150 under the title Fast Transformer Decoding.
The historical discussion links the same arXiv paper as its source for MQA.
The discussion of compressed and sparse global attention links the model card as its source.
With equal-size entries and 512 reads per query in both designs, writing one entry per token stores about four times as many entries as writing one per four tokens.
